candidate.long_definition: a log is a timestamped line that software writes while it runs — request received, job started, order failed, retry scheduled. think of it like the entries a nurse or pharmacist adds to a patient's chart as care happens: each line says when it happened, what the system did, and enough context to reconstruct the event later without exposing anything sensitive.
candidate.why_it_matters: when something breaks, the log is where the software tells you what it actually did, not what you assumed from the screen. in an EHR downtime or a failed interface, IT will pull the logs the same way you'd pull an MAR to see what was really given — stop guessing from the UI and read the receipts.
candidate.example_in_sentence: the vendor checked the interface log and saw the pharmacy order never reached the dispensing cabinet because the message was missing the patient's location.

items.job: registered nurse on a medical-surgical unit at a community hospital, 12-hour day shifts

candidate.long_definition: observability is how a team can tell what a software system is actually doing from the outside, without cracking it open. it comes from three main feeds: logs (a running record of events), metrics (numbers tracked over time, like response speed or error counts), and traces (the path a single request takes through the system). dashboards and alerts turn those feeds into something humans can watch, so operators spot trouble before users complain.
candidate.why_it_matters: this is the "can we actually see what's happening?" capability — a lot like how continuous monitoring on a patient tells you something is wrong before the patient codes. when an outage hits, the gap between a five-minute fix and a two-hour scramble is usually whether the team set this up ahead of time.
candidate.example_in_sentence: IT said once they added better observability on the charting system, they could see the login slowdowns on night shift instead of waiting for nurses to call the help desk.

items.job: staff pharmacist at a neighborhood retail pharmacy

candidate.long_definition: observability is how a team sees what a system is doing from the outside without opening it up. logs record individual events (this prescription was sent, this claim was rejected), metrics track numbers over time (claims per hour, average response time), and traces follow a single request through every step it touched. dashboards and alerts surface trouble before users start calling.
candidate.why_it_matters: this is the "can we actually tell what happened?" capability. when the pharmacy system goes down mid-shift, the difference between a five-minute fix and a two-hour one is usually whether the vendor set this up ahead of time. teams add logs and metrics before anything is obviously broken, the same way federal law requires a full count of every controlled substance at the end of each shift.
candidate.example_in_sentence: the release notes said they added better observability around claim adjudication, so the help desk can now see exactly where a rejection stalled.

items.job: clinical pharmacist at a 300-bed community hospital

candidate.long_definition: observability is how an IT team sees what a system is actually doing from the outside, without cracking it open. logs record events (what happened), metrics track numbers over time (how often, how fast, how many), and traces follow a single request through all the pieces it touches. dashboards and alerts surface trouble before users start calling to report it.
candidate.why_it_matters: this is the "can we tell what the system is doing right now?" capability. much like you wouldn't manage a septic patient without vitals, labs, and a trend over time, IT can't troubleshoot a clinical app without this instrumentation in place beforehand. when the EHR hiccups mid-shift, good observability turns a two-hour mystery into a five-minute fix.
candidate.example_in_sentence: the vendor promised better observability in the next release so downtime notices would stop being the first sign that order entry was failing.
